newsitem.title: USA: Dow ends up after Greenspan speech roils market.
newsitem.headline: Dow ends up after Greenspan speech roils market.

text.p: U.S. stocks ended higher on Friday after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan seized center stage with comments on the economy and interest rates.
The first moments of the session saw a flurry of activity, as investors struggled to divine the Fed's next move from a speech delivered by Greenspan in New York late Thursday.
But stocks quickly settled back into a narrow trading range, as Wall Street once again found nothing in the way of conclusive evidence in the Fed Chairman's comments.
The Dow gained 33 points to end unofficially at 7170.

"I think people can read whatever it is they wanted to in his comments," said Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter. "He did allude to some good things happening, but there was really nothing new here."
Indeed, it seemed that Greenspan's speech included at least one warning to offset every piece of good news.

He spent much of the speech defending the Fed's March interest rate increase, pointing to the need for the Fed to act pre-emptively against inflation risks. But he also cast some doubt whether such a need existed now.
"To be sure, 1997 is not 1994 when the Fed was forced to tighten monetary conditions very substantially to avoid accommodating rising inflation," Greenspan said.
It was in 1994 and early 1995 that the Fed adopted seven interest rate increases, doubling short-term rates to six percent from three percent in the process.

While analysts are divided on whether the Fed will pause before moving again on rates, many argue that regardless of the next move, the stock market's recent rebound has taken prices to a level where risks likely outweigh rewards over the near term.
"We're definitely cautious here," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "The risk right now is to the downside rather than to the upside."

With wholesale and retail price, industrial production and housing starts reports all due next week and the Fed's May 20 meeting drawing closer, analysts said the market would likely resume its choppy pattern, living statistic to statistic.
The Dow's gains brought its advance for the week to 98.33 points.
In individual issues, Cephalon Inc slid seven points to 13 after a Food and Drug Administration panel recommended against approving Myotrophin, the company's treatment for Lou Gehrig's disease.
Chiron Corp, Cephalon's development partner for the drug, fell 7/8 to 19-1/8.

Intel Corp gained 3/4 to 159-1/2. Late today, the company said a design flaw in its Pentium II and Pentium Pro processors could be fixed with software and would not require a mass recall of the chips.
Ball Corp fell 1-3/8 to 26-1/8 after the shares were downgraded to neutral by Morgan Stanley.
Clayton Homes Inc fell 3/4 to 13-5/8 and Oakwood Homes Corp fell 3/8 to 21 after Oppenheimer & Co lowered its ratings on both companies.
The S&P 500 rose 4.52 points to 824.78.
The Nasdaq Composite gained 4.22 points to 1335.05.
((-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730))
